paper_metadata.title: High temperature oxidation behaviour of single crystal superalloys RR 3000 and CMSX-4

evidence.quote: This paper describes the oxidation behaviour of two technologically important nickel based superalloys, RR3000 and CMSX-4, used extensively in gas turbine blade applications.

The results of the XRD and SEM/EDX analyses presented in the previous section indicated that upon exposure to air at 1100 uC, a mixed oxide scale was formed on the surface of the single crystal superalloys.

However, spallation of the scale, during cooling, subsequently occurred. The extent of spallation was found to increase gradually over 20 h of oxidation and then intensified to a point where only small portions of the scale remained adherent to the underlying metal (Fig. 3).
The most likely reason for stress relaxation was believed to be microcracking in the alumina layer.

It is believed to be due to the tensile stresses developed in the scales by the large shrinkage in volume (,9%) accompanying the transformation of alumina from the metastable h phase to the stable a phase.
After the formation of a mixed oxide scale, the activity of oxygen at the metal/oxide interface may decrease, facilitating the selective oxidation of aluminium.
It is obvious from the results obtained from the test samples (Fig. 3) that spallation of the scale is the major process impairing the resistance of alloy RR3000 to oxidation at high temperatures.

evidence.quote: Meanwhile, solid phase reactions among the initial simple oxides led to the formation of more complex oxides, including NiCr2O4, CrTaO4, AlTaO4 and NiCoAl2O4.
At 1100 uC, the much higher growth rate of NiO as compared with that of the other oxides resulted in the overgrowth of NiO crystals.
This was believed to be due to the loss by vaporisation of the Re oxide, Re2O7, which has a high vapour pressure at high temperatures.
